pages.text: Air presses on everything, about 1,013 hectopascals at sea level, the weight of the whole column above. Torricelli found it in 1643: a tube of mercury stood upside down in a dish falls to about 760 millimetres and holds there.
pages.title: Barometers

pages.text: Here, as in the world, it thins as you climb, some 12 hPa for every hundred blocks up, and it sinks over hot ground, hot air rising off it.

It also moves with the weather. In a long fair spell the glass stands high; through the quarter day before rain it falls, near 20 hPa; under rain it sits low and lower in thunder, and it climbs again as the storm ends.
Admiral FitzRoy put barometers in fishing harbours in the 1860s on that rule: a falling glass foretells foul weather.

The mercury barometer is a wheel barometer: the mercury's float turns a dial on a cord, and a comparator reads its pressure from 940 to 1,060 hPa. The barograph is Vidie's aneroid capsule of 1844 inking a clockwork drum.

It keeps an hour of its own readings, its goggles say which way the glass is going and how fast, and its comparator gives a storm warning: nothing in steady weather, rising to 15 as the fall nears 4 hPa an hour.
